text: A doctor tells a young rodeo rider that his skull will not survive another fall. The Rider begins from that sentence instead of arriving at it. Brady is good with horses in a way that is hard to convert into any other job: the gentling and the training are the work, the riding was the future, and one injury takes both. Chloé Zhao stays with the practical business of it, a rope and a fence and an animal turning in a ring, patiently enough that the line between skill and recklessness stops being obvious. The men Brady grew up among keep measuring a person by what he can still climb onto. Rotterdam's audience voted it their award, which suits a film whose crisis is whether a man will take medical advice. A western in which the danger is the horse, not another man.

Brothers driving cattle stop for one night in Tombstone; by morning one of them is dead and the herd is gone. Revenge is the official business of the next ninety-seven minutes, and John Ford is in no hurry about it. The killing puts a surviving brother behind a badge, and a badge means a town rather than a pursuit: streets to walk, meals to sit through, a courtship carried on at the pace of a man with the whole evening free. The genres filed against the picture, western and drama and romance and history, are a fair account of how the running time actually goes, the reckoning postponed while the town gets on with being a town. It sits in the National Film Registry as an American document, one way of saying that the killing matters less than the settlement growing up around it. The shooting comes. It waits.

Shin-ae arrives in her late husband's hometown intending to belong there, and the town is too ordinary to allow it. Nobody is cruel to her. The neighbours are helpful, the streets are sunlit, and nothing in the place is dramatic enough to account for why she cannot settle into it. Lee Chang-dong takes a hundred and forty-three minutes over this, and the length is the method: what happens to Shin-ae comes not as a scene to be got through but as an accumulation of ordinary hours, well-meant advice, prayer offered as practical assistance. When Christianity gives her a vocabulary for her pain, the film takes the offer seriously rather than treating it as a target, which is what makes the argument she later picks so hard to dismiss. Almost everything rests on one face, held in frame past the point where a more tactful film would cut.

The fences came down under the weight of people who had not bought tickets, and after that the festival was improvising. Woodstock runs a hundred and eighty-four minutes, and much of that is spent away from the stage: the building of the site, the clearing of it afterwards, National Guard helicopters bringing food and medicine to an unplanned city of half a million. Michael Wadleigh's crew filmed performers taking drugs and the audience sliding around in mud, and none of it is arranged to flatter either party. The Academy's editing award is the honest description of the thing, three hours cut from a mountain of footage, with music left long enough to be heard as music rather than sampled. Between sets, concertgoers talk to the camera at length. The film treats them as the event.

One brother is leaving the triads; the other has just joined the police. Ninety-five minutes is not much room for that arrangement, and John Woo spends almost none of it on procedure: the debts and the old associates are a pretext for a film about men who cannot apologise in words and so do it with favours, gestures, and standing in front of each other at the wrong moment. The crime scenes are staged like arias. The family scenes play closer to a hospital visit, awkward and quiet and weighed down by obligation nobody will itemise. Hong Kong's film awards named it best film, which for a work built on gunfire is a verdict about the crying rather than the shooting. Loyalty is the only currency that clears here, and the exchange rate is punitive.

A teenager asks a classmate's father for advice on courting a teacher, and the man takes the question seriously. That is the joke, and also the trouble. Rushmore gives ninety-three minutes to a prep-school boy running an adult campaign on schoolboy resources, and Wes Anderson stages it so squarely, flat compositions and stage-managed manners, that Max's self-regard is visible without being mocked. The mismatch of scale does the comic work: large ambition, negligible standing, a first-grade teacher who has done nothing to deserve any of it. Then the friendship curdles into rivalry, and the film lets a boy and a grown man behave identically badly, which is less charming than it sounds and much better. Embarrassment is the engine. The consequences are visible several scenes before anyone inside the film notices them.

In Foshan, before the war, a martial arts family goes looking for an heir, and the search is conducted through formal challenges rather than turf. Ip Man moves through that etiquette for a while, and then history dispenses with it: the Second Sino-Japanese War scatters the schools, and by the later stretch of these hundred and thirty minutes he is in Hong Kong, trying to feed a family with a skill that has lost its market. Gong Er, who once fought him over her father's standing, is on an entirely different track, and Wong Kar-Wai keeps declining to let her story resolve into romance. The honours the film gathered are for photography and costume, which is fair: mastery registers here in a coat, a lamp, a stance held a half-second too long. Style, not plot, is the continuity.

The emperor dies, his son inherits, and in Rome that is less a succession than a demotion for everyone the father preferred. Maximus keeps an army's loyalty and loses all legal standing, which lands him in the arena, where, as the film is careful to state, men kill each other for the amusement of paying audiences. That commercial detail organises the whole hundred and fifty-five minutes. Ridley Scott shoots spectacle as an industry: promoters, gate money, a crowd whose approval can be bought retail and never quite controlled. The Best Picture Oscar went to it, and the sentiment that won it is unembarrassed, the politics deliberately plain. What the film understands precisely is the price of a roar to a man who cannot rule without one.

The Winter Palace has more rooms than any plot could use, and Aleksandr Sokurov uses them as rooms. A ghost and a French marquis walk through it, one unseen and one increasingly opinionated, and the building supplies its own history out of order: a court in one doorway, a war down the corridor, a ball that seems unsure of its own date. The European Film Award for direction is the accurate honour, because for ninety-nine minutes the only real question is where the camera goes next and who it passes. Nothing is annotated. The marquis's complaints, about taste, about Russians, about what he is being shown, stand in for explanation. The effect is less that of a costume drama than of being walked round a house by someone with strong feelings about every wall.

A lawyer nobody hires takes the one case he cannot bill for. Song Woo-seok's practice is going nowhere when a friend's son is arrested, falsely accused and tortured, and The Attorney spends a hundred and twenty-seven minutes turning a self-interested man into a litigator against the state that licensed him. The interrogation passages are hard to sit with; the courtroom passages are built as procedure, objection by objection, since what was produced under torture still has to be disqualified in the correct order. Yang Woo-suk directs without irony, and the speeches are unmistakably speeches. It took the Blue Dragon award for best film. The real subject is smaller than justice: a man finding out what his own competence is for.

A farmer works out what he owes, weighs it against what a city pays, and takes his son to Calcutta to close the difference. The land is two bighas of family ground and a corporation wants it; Bimal Roy never lets that figure turn symbolic, keeping it a sum to be raised by a date, in a place where a day of labour buys less than a day of living. The boy stays in frame throughout, which alters the measure of everything, since each delay is counted against a child's patience rather than a man's pride. Filmfare named it best film, though the picture has no appetite for triumph; it is organised around fares, wages, and small amounts of money moving the wrong way. It travels at the speed of a man who cannot afford to ride.

Mardar comes out of prison and finds a woman with his lost lover's face, then refuses to accept coincidence. Three years earlier he had tried to abduct that lover; now he is standing in front of someone who may or may not be her, and Lou Ye treats the double as a practical difficulty rather than a metaphysical one: if there is a lie, whose, and if there is not, where did three years go. Eighty-three minutes is a short allowance for a love story, and the brevity keeps it at street level, a matter of who owes whom an explanation and who is following whom along a river. The Tiger Award at Rotterdam went to it. The romance behaves throughout like a missing-persons enquiry, more interested in searching than in what is found.

Denji fights devils for wages and falls in love in the same shift. Reze Arc lifts one stretch of a serialised story into a hundred theatrical minutes, which puts an unusual squeeze on the material: a courtship and an escalation have to share the same scenes, and the animation has to make a nervous conversation land as hard as a fight in which nothing is off limits. Tatsuya Yoshihara plays it for volume, and the premise is candid about the arrangement: affection is a tactic here, and survival is not governed by rules anyone can appeal to. It arrived to an audience that already knew the terms. It is not an entry point and does not pretend to be one, starting instead from a world already built and spending its length raising the cost of living there.

Nuclear detonators reach the west of Ireland concealed in a six-pack of Beamish. They arrive in the luggage of an American tourist who flew over to meet a woman from the internet and whose only relevant qualification is kickboxing. Moving Target was made for television in 2000, runs eighty-six minutes, and arranges its chase around three parties who all want the same carton: the IRA, US intelligence, and the Garda Síochána. Paul Ziller plays the premise entirely straight, which is the only way it can function, since the comedy of the setup would dissolve the thriller and the thriller is what the running time is for. Ireland's west supplies the geography a spy plot usually takes from capitals. The whole thing is over before the coincidence has to be defended.
